Title: Fix Tenable One findings where developers work: Tenable and OpenAI Daybreak Defense Factory
Context: OpenAI built the connector, one of the select supported integrations in the OpenAI Daybreak Defense Factory
Full Text:
Tenable One customers can now bring selected findings into OpenAI Daybreak Defense Factory through a local Codex Security CLI import with Tenable’s description and solution attached, so developers can fix them where they already work. OpenAI built the connector, one of the select supported integrations in the OpenAI Daybreak Defense Factory.

Key takeaways

Code security findings often lose their context in the handoff. Security teams pass code findings to developers as exports and tickets, and developers end up reinvestigating before they can fix anything.

Daybreak Defense Factory imports selected Tenable One findings. OpenAI built a Tenable One connector into Codex Security, which OpenAI publishes as open source. The connector reads findings through the Inventory Export API in Tenable One or from CSV exports. Each finding arrives in the local Codex Security workbench with its name, severity and state, plus Tenable’s description and solution.

You can try it today with OpenAI’s setup guide. Select a code repository and its findings in Tenable One, export them, then preview and import them into Codex Security against your local checkout of the repository.

Why code findings stall between security and development

A vulnerability often takes an indirect path from the security team that finds it to the developer who fixes it, and important context gets lost along the way. The security team sends the finding over as an export or a ticket, where a development team triages it. When a developer finally picks it up, they still have to work out which code is affected and what a good fix looks like before they can write a line of code to fix it. Most of that context already existed on the security side. It just didn’t make the trip.

We think the fix should start where the developer already works. That’s the idea behind Tenable One’s integration with OpenAI Daybreak Defense Factory: the security team selects findings in Tenable One, and the developer imports them locally with the Codex Security CLI, with Tenable’s description and solution attached when available. Each finding keeps its Tenable finding ID, and its file path and line number when the export includes them.

What Daybreak Defense Factory imports from Tenable One

The findings come from code repository assets in the Tenable One Exposure Management Platform inventory. Each one carries its name, severity, and state, along with Tenable’s description of the issue and Tenable’s solution.

After the import, the Daybreak Defense Factory is designed to help the developer investigate the affected code, decide which findings to prioritize, and propose a fix in the code.

Import Tenable One findings into your Defense Factory in four steps

To try it today, OpenAI’s setup guide walks you through a local command-line import:

Select the repository and findings. In the Tenable One inventory, open the Code Repository asset and copy its asset ID and the IDs of the findings you want to import.

Export the selection. Export the asset and findings through the Inventory Export API (for tenants on cloud.tenable.com), or start from existing CSV exports. The guide’s export helper checks that each finding belongs to the selected asset. If your export includes file paths and line numbers, the guide shows how to keep them in the import.

Preview, then save. Run codex-security publish findings --provider tenable with --dry-run against your local checkout to preview the import. When the preview looks right, run it again without --dry-run and confirm to save the findings.

Read the import back. Run codex-security findings imported to list what Codex Security saved, with each Tenable finding ID and the “not assessed” status that Codex Security gives it at the start.

To refresh the findings later, import again with the same --source-key value, a tenant alias, plus the asset ID. According to the guide, Codex Security updates the evidence for findings that changed and keeps identical findings as they are.

Get started

OpenAI’s setup guide has the full commands, the helper scripts, and the CSV formats.

Title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Frequently asked questions about OpenJDK remote code execution vulnerability
Context: Later that day, Oracle released its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU), and the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group published its own advisory
Full Text:
Java4Shell is a flaw in how Java decodes Base64 data. Calif, which found it, says it can let attackers run code on widely used Java applications without logging in. Oracle released fixed Java builds on November 17, and Calif is withholding its exploits for individual applications for now.

Key takeaways

CVE-2026-114938, dubbed Java4Shell, is an OpenJDK memory corruption vulnerability that Oracle scores 8.1 on CVSS 3.1, and Calif says its testing showed attackers could run code without logging in on applications such as Atlassian Jira and Jenkins.

As of November 17, Tenable is not aware of any reports that attackers have exploited this flaw, though Calif has published a PoC that triggers the bug without taking control of the system and a second researcher reports building a working exploit.

Oracle released fixed builds on November 17, and according to Calif, only systems running an affected Java version on x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 VBMI can be affected.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding Java4Shell, a vulnerability in OpenJDK that was patched on November 17, 2026.

FAQ

When was Java4Shell first disclosed?

On November 17, security firm Calif said on X that it had found and reported the flaw, and that details of Java4Shell, as Calif named it, had leaked ahead of a fix. Later that day, Oracle released its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU), and the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group published its own advisory. Calif then published its technical write-up. Oracle credits Quang Luong of Calif.io and Albert Yang for reporting the vulnerability.

Since the vulnerability has leaked: Calif discovered and reported Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938).We're publishing technical details by 1 PM Pacific today, after Oracle releases a patch.Stay tuned! https://t.co/No5hJXK1Zx

— Calif (@calif_io) November 17, 2026

What is CVE-2026-114938?

CVE

Description

CVSSv3.1

CVE-2026-114938

OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Memory Corruption Vulnerability (Java4Shell)

8.1

CVE-2026-114938 is a memory corruption vulnerability in the part of Java that decodes Base64, a common format that applications use to send data such as login details and file uploads. Oracle assigned it a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1 and rates its attack complexity as high. Calif says it scores 9.2 under CVSS 4.0. An attacker does not need to log in to exploit it remotely. According to Oracle, the flaw can only be exploited when an application passes untrusted data to the affected Java APIs, such as through a web service.

Is CVE-2026-114938 among the Java fixes in Oracle's November 2026 CSPU?

Yes. CVE-2026-114938 is addressed by one of the 11 Java SE security patches in Oracle's November 2026 CSPU, released November 17. For a breakdown of all the patches in this release, see our blog post on Oracle's November 2026 CSPU.

What is known about CVE-2026-114938?

The flaw is in a performance shortcut that Java uses to decode Base64 data faster on certain Intel and AMD processors. When the shortcut receives a specially crafted Base64 string, it writes data beyond the memory it set aside. That can corrupt other information the application is holding in memory.

According to Calif, an attacker can use this flaw in two ways. The first, which Calif calls "JavaBleed," lets an attacker read the application's memory. That memory may hold secrets such as keys and tokens. The second lets an attacker run their own code on the server. Calif also says that each application needs its own exploit, and that a failed attempt can crash the application, though an attacker can often try again.

Exposure depends on the processor as well as the Java version. According to Calif, Java uses the affected code only on x86-64 processors that support a feature called AVX-512 VBMI. These include Intel Xeon processors from the Granite Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Sapphire Rapids and Ice Lake families, as well as AMD processors based on Zen 4 or newer. Calif says systems with ARM64 processors are not affected. On Linux, a system meets this requirement when its processor reports all four of the avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi and bmi2 flags.

Which versions of Java are affected?

The OpenJDK Vulnerability Group lists the Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 release lines as affected by CVE-2026-114938. Calif says OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer are affected. Oracle lists the following Oracle builds as affected:

Oracle GraalVM for JDK

Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition

Oracle lists only builds it supports and says earlier versions are likely also affected. The Java 8 build on Oracle's list is its Enterprise Performance Pack. The OpenJDK advisory does not list standard Java 8 or Java 11 as affected by this vulnerability.

I don't use Oracle's Java builds. Am I affected?

Possibly. The flaw is in OpenJDK code, and according to Calif, the following Java distributions built from OpenJDK are also vulnerable:

Eclipse Temurin

Each vendor releases fixed builds on its own schedule, so check with your distribution's vendor for its fixed versions.

Which applications are known to be affected?

Calif says its initial testing showed that an attacker could run their own code on the following applications in their default configurations, when they run on an affected version of Java on a processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI. The list is not exhaustive, according to Calif.

Calif also said it ran its own code on sample applications built on frameworks including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Calif adds that everyday functions, including authentication and file uploads, can lead to the vulnerable code, so more applications than the ones Calif tested may be exposed. Calif says researcher samczsun gave it a client-side exploit, and that a Java program can be compromised when it connects over TLS to a server an attacker controls, even if the program offers no service of its own. Calif says it will publish its exploits for individual products at a later date.

Has Java4Shell been exploited in the wild?

As of November 17, we are not aware of any reports of exploitation of CVE-2026-114938, and it is not listed in the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available?

Yes. Calif published a PoC alongside its write-up that triggers the flaw without taking control of the system. It shows whether a given Java version and processor reproduce the bug. It does not show whether a particular application is exposed.

On November 17, Kevin Breen of Immersive said on X that they had developed a working exploit for CVE-2026-114938. According to Breen, the exploit has to be adapted to each application. It works only on a vulnerable version of Java running on a processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI, and only against applications that decode Base64 data. Breen also said that Apache Tomcat's Basic authentication and the java-jwt library provide ways to exploit the flaw before a user logs in. The post does not say that the exploit has been released.

Are there any mitigations?

Calif identified two Java startup options that keep the vulnerable code from running. The first, -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, turns off the Base64 shortcut. The second, -XX:UseAVX=2, turns off AVX-512 instructions. According to Calif, the second option applies only to x86-64 systems, and Java on ARM processors fails to start with it. Neither Oracle nor the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group mentions these options in its advisory.

Yes. CISA's KEV catalog includes 13 vulnerabilities in Oracle Java SE and the Java Runtime Environment (JRE), six of which are known to have been used in ransomware campaigns. Those six are:

Has Tenable Research classified this vulnerability as part of Vulnerability Watch?

Yes. CVE-2026-114938 has been classified as a "Vulnerability of Interest" as part of Vulnerability Watch.

Are Tenable products affected by this vulnerability?

Tenable is aware of this vulnerability and is investigating whether it affects any Tenable products.

Has Tenable released any product coverage for this vulnerability?

A list of Tenable plugins for this vulnerability can be found on the individual CVE page for CVE-2026-114938 as they're released. This link will display all available plugins for this vulnerability, including upcoming plugins in our Plugins Pipeline.

How can Tenable customers find affected assets?

Tenable One Vulnerability Management customers can go to Explore > Software to view installed software across their assets, then filter by product name and version to look for Java installations to compare against the affected versions above. Exposure also depends on the processor, as described above. Software data comes from credentialed and agent scans. For details, see Use the Software Page.

Tenable One Vulnerability Management customers can also use the Java Visibility and Exposures report, which lists Java installations and the hosts where they were detected.

Tenable One Attack Surface Management customers can find internet-facing assets running Java with the filter Programming Languages contains Java. Those assets can then be scanned with other Tenable sensors to check whether they are affected by CVE-2026-114938.

Title: Oracle November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update Addresses 640 CVEs (CVE-2026-114938)
Context: 8% of all patches Background On November 17, Oracle released its Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) for November 2026
Full Text:
Oracle addresses 640 CVEs in its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update with 655 patches, including 62 critical updates.

Key Takeaways

The November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) contains fixes for 640 unique CVEs in 655 security updates

62 issues (9.5% of all patches) were assigned a critical severity rating

Oracle Hyperion received the highest number of patches at 267, accounting for 40.8% of all patches

Background

On November 17, Oracle released its Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) for November 2026. Beginning in May 2026, Oracle introduced CSPUs as a monthly release cycle that sits between the larger quarterly Critical Patch Updates (CPUs), addressing a focused set of high-severity issues on a faster cadence. This CSPU contains fixes for 640 unique CVEs in 655 security updates across 21 Oracle product families. Out of the 655 security updates published, 9.5% of patches were assigned a critical severity. Medium severity patches accounted for the bulk of security patches at 41.8%, followed by high severity patches at 38%.

This month's update includes 62 critical patches across 57 CVEs.

Several of the third-party components (OpenSSL, curl, 7-Zip, Microsoft SQL Server 2019, node-forge) were found to contain vulnerabilities, and updated versions have been made available by the providers.

Title: Tenable One Adversary View brings Claude Mythos’ adversarial reasoning to your environment
Context: Adversary View is a capability within Tenable One that analyzes existing scan data to identify viable vulnerability chains and the specific routes an attacker could take through...
Full Text:
Tenable One Adversary View is now generally available. Powered by Claude Mythos, it reads your scan data like an attacker would and tells you what to fix first.

Key takeaways

Adversary View is generally available. Tenable One customers with Tenable Hexa AI can run it today, with nothing new to deploy.

Tenable Hexa AI applies Claude Mythos’ adversarial reasoning to data you already collect. It works across the findings from your existing scans and plugins to find vulnerability chains and attack-path choke points.

Break more attack paths with fewer fixes. Adversary View ranks every fix by how many attack paths it stops, so your team can prioritize actions that cut off the most attacker progress.

Virtually every security team works from the same question: What can we fix next to reduce the most risk? Tenable One is designed to answer this question every day with attack path analysis, which uses rule-based logic to continuously map how attackers could reach your critical assets.

Tenable One Adversary View, now live for all Tenable Hexa AI users, adds a deeper, point-in-time check on top of it. Tenable Hexa AI uses Claude’s Mythos-class model to reason like an adversary across your existing scan data, working through how findings combine instead of matching them to predefined rules. Then it points you to the fixes that cut off the most routes.

When Tenable previewed Adversary View in September, we promised a way to see your environment the way an attacker does. If you’re a Tenable One customer with Tenable Hexa AI, you can run it today.

Vulnerability management programs must adapt to AI-accelerated discovery

AI is reshaping vulnerability management by accelerating vulnerability discovery and the creation of working exploits.

For security teams, every new CVE makes it harder to answer the question: “What do we fix next?” These teams still need to understand whether a new CVE applies to their environment, whether they can validate it, and whether anyone is exploiting it. Only then can they start to prioritize it against the thousands of other vulnerabilities across their environment.

But an attacker doesn’t start with a CVSS-sorted spreadsheet of your vulnerabilities. Attackers read the environment to determine which hosts talk to each other, what services are exposed, and which accounts are reachable. Then they reason about how to get from an entry point to a valuable asset.

Severity-based prioritization doesn’t operate that way. A netstat entry, a mapped network drive, or a line buried in plugin output may not be a critical finding on its own, but together they can form a dangerous attack path.

Spotting those combinations across every vulnerability, at this volume, is more than any team can do by hand. Keeping up requires automated attack path analysis, assisted by frontier AI, for prioritization and remediation.

What Adversary View does

Adversary View, accessible in Tenable Hexa AI, looks at your assets from an attacker’s viewpoint. Point Adversary View at a set of assets you already scan and ask how an attacker could move through them.

Tenable Hexa AI uses Claude Mythos to apply adversarial reasoning, building an on-demand graph of your environment from your existing vulnerability scan data, with no new sensors or agents needed, and returns:

Ranked vulnerability chains, with each hop backed by scan evidence

Choke points, and a prioritized list of what to fix, ordered by how many paths each fix closes rather than by severity alone

Remediation and reporting includes patches and configuration changes for each route, plus a Jira ticket, remediation dashboard, or shareable PDF report

Attack path analysis and Adversary View cover different jobs. Attack path analysis watches your environment continuously and flags paths based on pre-defined rules as they form.

Adversary View is the on-demand deep read: Scope it to a business unit or a tag, and Tenable Hexa AI reasons through that slice of your environment the way an attacker would.

Adversary View in action

We ran Adversary View across a production environment of hosts, and it found and prioritized numerous paths to a crown-jewel asset. The top-ranked path starts at an internet-facing host, moves through a workstation and a domain controller, and ends at a Windows Server 2016 box still vulnerable to EternalBlue, the exploit behind WannaCry.

Adversary View also found a short list of fixes that closes nearly all of the paths: patch two servers (a domain controller and a second Windows Server 2022 box) and you block Server Message Block (SMB) traffic from the internet into the internal network. That one firewall rule closes 32 SMB connections that offer a direct path from the internet into the internal network.

Adversary View is a capability within Tenable One that analyzes existing scan data to identify viable vulnerability chains and the specific routes an attacker could take through connected assets. It is accessed through Tenable Hexa AI and operates as a point-in-time inspection. To begin, the user opens Tenable Hexa AI and selects the Adversary View card. This triggers the agent to analyze scan data and construct a graph of asset connections. The scope can be set to all assets or narrowed to specific tags, IP ranges, or business units. Once submitted, Tenable Hexa AI offers to tag the scoped asset group for future reference. After confirming your scoped assets, Adversary View deterministically builds a map and applies reasoning to discover vulnerability chains without relying on predefined rules. The model interrogates the asset graph step-by-step to identify paths an attacker could traverse. The output includes an executive summary that identifies structural chokepoints and the fixes that are aimed at reducing the most risk. In the example shown, Tenable Hexa AI identified and ranked seven viable attack routes reaching crown-jewel assets. The top-ranked route traces an attacker’s movement from an internet-facing workstation to an EternalBlue-vulnerable server. Each step in a route is backed by actual scan output, including active network connections (NETSTAT_CONN) and specific CVEs, grounding findings in real data. A “What to Fix” section provides tailored remediation recommendations for each route, specifying control changes that disrupt the attacker path across multiple hops. Users can interact with Tenable Hexa AI through follow-up prompts to prioritize fixes and assess risk reduction before applying patches. Tenable Hexa AI is designed to surface the top highest-leverage actions that eliminate maximum exposure. From the conversation, users can create a Jira ticket or Exposure Response initiative directly, with Tenable Hexa AI collecting the technical details needed and allowing the user to define scope before pushing findings into the IT Service Management (ITSM) console.

How to run Adversary View in your environment

Here’s how to run the same analysis on your own assets.

Start a conversation. Open Tenable Hexa AI and click the “Adversary View” tile, or ask for an Adversary View in your own words.

Set your scope. The demo uses the “All Assets” option. In your own environment, you can target tags, IP ranges, operating systems, or a business unit. Tenable Hexa AI offers to tag the scoped assets so you can rerun the same analysis later.

Confirm and let it run. Click “Confirm”. Tenable Hexa AI builds a map of how your scoped assets connect, then uses Claude Mythos to reason across that map and the raw scan evidence behind it. The analysis takes several minutes and keeps running in the background if you leave the panel.

Read the summary. Results open with an executive summary that includes the top vulnerability chains in your environment and the fixes designed to stop them.

Inspect a route. Each ranked route shows its hops on a graph, with the scan evidence behind every hop, from SMB sessions and netstat connections to specific CVEs.

Find the fixes that matter most. Each route lists patches and configuration changes that help to stop attacks. Ask Tenable Hexa AI follow-up questions to see which fixes close the most routes at once.

Turn it into tracked work. Ask Tenable Hexa AI to open a Jira ticket or track your remediation efforts by creating a dashboard. It gathers the technical details, then pushes them into your IT Service Management (ITSM) console.

Generate a report. Have Tenable Hexa AI generate a PDF and download it straight from the chat. The report summarizes all findings and top actions so you can share results across teams.

Prompts to try

Show me an adversary view for assets tagged “production”.

Show me the shortest path from any public entry point to a Critical ACR asset.

Show me the top 3 choke points and explain why each ranks where it does.

If I could only patch 5 assets this sprint, which ones should I pick to close the most vulnerability chains?

Prompts to follow up with

Create JIRA tickets with the top fix and assign them to respective owners.

Ensure MacOS assets are in the appropriate Smart Group to ensure remediation of [CHOKE POINT] in the next patching window.

Create a downloadable PDF for all discovered vulnerability chains.

How to get started with Adversary View

Before your first run, check that you have:

A Tenable One Foundation or Tenable One Advanced license

“Frontier AI Model Access” turned on in Tenable Hexa AI’s settings by your admin

A role with access: Adversary View is on by default for administrators and scan managers, and custom roles need the right permissions

Scans covering your target assets with the options “Override normal verbosity” enabled and “Report as much information as possible” selected

Get more details about Adversary View

Ready to see which of your vulnerabilities an attacker could chain together, and which fixes stop them?

Read the documentation

Existing customers: Open Tenable Hexa AI in Tenable One and click the Adversary View tile.

New to Tenable One? Request a demo.

Elevation of Privilege (EoP) vulnerabilities accounted for 48.9% of the vulnerabilities patched this month, followed by remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities at 27.1%.

Moderate

CVE-2026-124194 | Microsoft Outlook spoofing vulnerability

CVE-2026-124194 is a spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook. It received a CVSSv3 score of 6.5 and is rated moderate. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by convincing a target to open a crafted Microsoft Office file. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to obtain the target’s valid NTLMv2 hash, which can then be used to impersonate that user in follow-on attacks.

According to Microsoft, this vulnerability was exploited in the wild as a zero-day. Additionally, the advisory credits this discovery to a security researcher that used Claude, the large language model (LLM) from Anthropic, though no specific version of Claude was noted in the advisory.

Critical

CVE-2026-118146 | Windows Active Directory Domain Services remote code execution vulnerability

CVE-2026-118146 is an RCE vulnerability affecting Windows Active Directory Domain Services. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.8 and is rated as critical. An authenticated attacker could exploit an incorrect authorization in Active Directory Domain Services to execute code over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on the affected system. It was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

Important

CVE-2026-120002 | Microsoft SharePoint Server elevation of privilege vulnerability

CVE-2026-120002 is an EoP vulnerability affecting Microsoft SharePoint Server. It received a CVSSv3 score of 9.9 and is rated as important. An authenticated attacker could exploit an incorrect authorization in Microsoft Office SharePoint to elevate privileges over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to gain elevated privileges. It was assessed as “Exploitation Less Likely.”

Critical

CVE-2026-118207 | Microsoft Exchange Server remote code execution vulnerability

CVE-2026-118207 is an RCE vulnerability affecting Microsoft Exchange Server. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.8 and is rated as critical. An authenticated attacker could send malformed input to Microsoft Exchange Server, causing code to execute over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on the affected system. It was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

Critical

CVE-2026-119952 | Windows Schannel remote code execution vulnerability

CVE-2026-119952 is an RCE vulnerability affecting Windows Schannel. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.1 and is rated as critical. An unauthenticated attacker could exploit an observable timing discrepancy in Windows Schannel to execute code over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on the affected system. It was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

Title: php2shell one week later: Why one exploit doesn’t work everywhere
Context: What can we learn from this Inevitably, when a remote code execution vulnerability is discovered in a broadly deployed core component of the services we use, a knee-jerk...
Full Text:
php2shell raised fears of mass exploitation. A week of testing by our research team found that working exploits had to be fitted to each target’s exact PHP setup. Systems that share one build, such as network appliances, are the exception: one tuned exploit can reach every device that runs it.

Key takeaways

The five vulnerable PHP sites we exposed to the internet were not compromised, and public proofs-of-concept (PoCs) that go beyond version checks do not reliably confirm whether a host is vulnerable. Exploitation has been confirmed elsewhere, on researcher honeypots and on some network appliances.

In realistic environments, turning php2shell into remote code execution usually takes an exploit built for the specific target. That is hard, not impossible, and it puts php2shell in a different category from Log4Shell, even though both received near-maximum severity ratings. Where many systems share one build, such as network appliances, a single calibrated exploit can work against all of them.

Patch now, starting with internet-facing management interfaces, network appliances, and end-of-life PHP branches. Tenable Nessus and Tenable One Web App Scanning have had version-based detection since October 21.

Background

On October 20, 2026, PHP announced two vulnerabilities, and on October 21 released fixes for flaws that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw. CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw caused by stale state shared between requests on the same worker. Each has a CVSSv4 score of 9.2. For a full breakdown of affected versions, fixes and mitigations, see our frequently asked questions blog post.

This post covers what happened after the disclosure, based on what our team observed directly.

From disclosure to headline in under 48 hours

php2shell got big fast. Details of the vulnerabilities leaked online before the official release. Within two days, the vulnerability had a name, a logo and coverage in mainstream media.

Several websites went offline as a precaution, as described in our threat actor response blog post. Censys’s php2shell dashboard, which tracks PHP services by reported version, showed about 30.3 million PHP services still on an affected version on October 29, though a matching version does not mean a system can be exploited.

The comparison with Log4Shell came up early, but the two are very different to exploit. With Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228), attackers only had to send a short piece of text to a vulnerable application, for example in a login form or a web request. If the application logged that text, the attack worked. The same text worked against almost any vulnerable target without changes, so attackers could launch it at scale within hours, and many of those attacks succeeded.

php2shell is different. Exploitation depends on the state of the heap, the process manager in use, worker reuse and how memory is laid out on a given build. php2shell drew attention quickly, but attackers can't exploit it as easily as Log4Shell.

What changed while we were testing

Several developments that matter for defenders came after our research began:

On October 24, honeypots run by Perplexity researcher Adel Karimi recorded 35 successful shell executions across three sensors running PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php with a single worker, a configuration that favors the exploit.

On October 26, CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Federal civilian agencies have until October 29 to remediate.

The same day, security firm Dream reported an attack chain that combined php2shell with a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw, Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300). Dream says the campaign rooted “25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea.” Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 says it independently verified the same attacker’s tooling and confirmed the reported results. We have not verified these findings ourselves.

On October 28, CISA added Fragnesia to the KEV catalog and noted that it can be chained with php2shell to run commands as root. By October 29, Palo Alto Networks reported active exploitation targeting internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces.

These reports are consistent with what we found. The exploit has to be calibrated to a specific build. Network appliances often run the same software across many devices, so one calibrated exploit can reach many of them. That is where we expect targeted exploitation to keep growing.

What we observed during our exploit research

Exposed targets

To measure real-world activity, we kept five vulnerable PHP sites reachable from the internet: four through the evening of October 24, and one still running in a standard, vulnerable configuration at the time of writing.

Over that period, we observed mass exploitation attempts that matched php2shell exploitation patterns. None of our targets had been compromised as of October 29.

Other organizations have reported exploitation attempts and, in the cases described above, successful exploitation. Amazon Threat Intelligence says php2shell is “now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild.” Our data does not contradict these reports. It shows that attempts, even at scale, were not enough to compromise a default installation in our environment. Attempts and successful compromises are two different numbers, and in the first days after a disclosure people often treat them as the same.

Public proofs-of-concept

We collected and tested almost all public PoCs. An early lead was php2shell poc, published by researcher Daniel Púa (devploit). It let us reproduce the exposure on multiple 8.4 and 8.5 environments with specific configurations. From there, we did deeper research, including white-box testing and code and patch comparison, and achieved remote code execution on PHP 7.4.33.

What we learned from this research is that the exploit inadvertently reveals a clean discriminator: the same multipart POST that begins stage 1 produces a different allocator response on patched vs. unpatched PHP. No heap corruption, no crash, no shell, just a measurable size difference in how the server handles the request. That became signal 1: a large filename in the multipart request produces a measurably different allocation size on vulnerable versions than on fixed versions, because the patched allocator rounds to a corrected size class. Same request, same PHP – different memory behavior depending solely on whether the UAF patch is present.

Tenable Research identified a second signal as well: the compact amplification sequences that exercise the UAF window's existence without triggering corruption. The session upload-progress oracle watches for the crash/recover pattern that vulnerable versions exhibit under controlled amplification.

These two signals became a stateful probe that a Nessus ‘direct check’ plugin could detect. However, the probe would miss some vulnerable systems and flag some patched ones as vulnerable.

The memory corruption is real, and PHP confirms memory disclosure as one of the impacts. Turning it into code execution on a target is difficult and unique to each target. Our working RCE required an exploit tuned to the target's environment, including its PHP build, SAPI, extensions and runtime configuration. A payload that works against one lab setup does not carry over to a different distribution package or a different PHP-FPM pool configuration.

AI-accelerated research: Useful, but it needs checking

AI agents sped up our reverse engineering and testing, and they also produced at least one convincing false positive. During a multi-hour session, an agent built a working shell against our PHP-FPM lab containers and reported it as confirmation of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. It was not. The agent had used a local file inclusion weakness that we had added to the lab, a different attack class that does not exist in default PHP deployments. A researcher caught the error by checking the exploit chain against the vulnerability's mechanics.

The lesson applies to anyone reading exploitation claims this week: a real shell is not proof that a specific CVE was used. We also ran into inconsistent responses from AI tools when doing authorized exploit validation, which slowed parts of the work.

White-box testing

The GDB analysis and heap geometry research below show why: there is no universal offset. Code execution is a real exposure yet it is not as simple as portrayed. The RCE we achieved on PHP 7.4.33 worked only once the exploit matched that one setup. A profile that achieves a shell against one lab container does not carry over to a different distribution package, a different PHP-FPM pool configuration, or a different memory limit.

The chunk-relative offsets pictured in the ‘heap geometry capture method’ visuals below reference _zend_array at chunk+0x572a0, arData at chunk+0x64b80. These values illustrate the measurement method and are specific to PHP 8.3.35 built from the docker-library bookworm image on amd64. A Debian-packaged PHP 8.3.35, or a PHP 8.3.35 built with different extensions, produces different chunk geometry values. We used GDB against the live worker to measure the actual values for a given target.

Our failure to show that mass exploitation is quick or easy does not make this vulnerability harmless. A well-resourced attacker who wants a specific target can build that exploit, and AI-assisted tooling shortens the time it takes. It does make mass exploitation of the Log4Shell kind much less likely. The exception is any population of systems that share one build, such as network appliances, where the cost of calibration is paid once.

Why exploitation is hard

When possible, Tenable Research releases exposure direct checks to help customers detect exploitable vulnerabilities within their environments. These direct checks depend on finding reliable and safe methods of exercising a vulnerability in a way that simulates an exploit without triggering any destructive actions. This typically involves first researching how to develop an exploit, then figuring out how to test that safely.

Our research found the php2shell exposure difficult to reproduce broadly, even with white-box testing and GDB attached to processes, and even with AI agents analyzing runtime memory and source code for weaknesses and leads in parallel. What we learned from this research helps to inform us on the practical realities of real-world exploitation:

php2shell is a multi-stage memory corruption chain. A direct check triggering an out-of-memory condition alone does not fully guarantee the asset is also exposed to remote code execution.

In-memory offsets are version and system specific. The chunk-relative structure offsets required for heap manipulation change with every PHP patch release and system/software combination. Gaps in an inventory of known offsets and platforms could make a vulnerable system look patched (false-negative).

The OOM trigger depends on application-controlled memory limits. Whether the condition fires depends on the configured memory_limit and on whether the application overrides it via ini_set, PHP_VALUE, or PHP_ADMIN_VALUE per-request directives.

The use-after-free requires reuse of the PHP worker across consecutive requests. Under mod_php, keep-alive pins a connection to one worker; under FPM, session affinity (PHPSESSID) is required. Both depend on SAPI and process-manager settings. For example, pm.max_requests recycles workers and breaks the use-after-free chain with no visible sign, so the check returns a false negative.

The exploit crashes PHP workers. Workers appear to respawn reliably, but a direct check that intentionally degrades performance could still affect production systems.

What can we learn from this

Inevitably, when a remote code execution vulnerability is discovered in a broadly deployed core component of the services we use, a knee-jerk reaction is triggered that creates significant fears of mass exploitation and extreme risk. While we do not want to downplay the dangers of this vulnerability, it is valuable to understand the practicalities of exploitation in the real world versus the fear that is built around a CVE during the regular news cycle. In this case, that nuance points remediation first at internet-facing assets, especially appliances such as network infrastructure management interfaces, and anything else that runs a common, basic deployment that reduces overall complexity.

Prioritization matters more as AI finds more vulnerabilities

Calif, OpenAI and Wiz are credited with finding php2shell. Calif says AI assisted the discovery. We expect the number of disclosed vulnerabilities to keep rising as these tools improve, and many of them will come with high base scores. Patching everything rated critical at the speed of the news cycle will not be possible.

Security teams need to understand what a vulnerability takes to exploit, not only how bad the worst case is:

Is there a public exploit that works without changes, or only a crash PoC?

Does exploitation depend on a non-default configuration, a specific build or prior access?

Is the vulnerable component reachable from the internet in your environment?

Has anyone observed successful compromise, as opposed to scanning?

Exploit prediction scores such as EPSS, Tenable's Vulnerability Priority Rating (VPR) and confirmed exploitation sources such as CISA's KEV catalog help answer these questions. They work better alongside an analysis of the vulnerability itself than in place of one.

Patch anyway

Our observations do not mean php2shell should be ignored. The conditions for exploitation exist, exploit development will improve and targeted attacks against high-value PHP applications are plausible. Updating to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or applying your distribution's fixed packages, remains the recommendation. For end-of-life branches, plan an upgrade. Until then, apply the configuration mitigations described in our FAQ and limit internet exposure, starting with appliance management interfaces. For network appliances, PHP version numbers do not apply: use your vendor's fixed build or its interim mitigations.

What we are recommending is a different order of work. Patch or isolate internet-facing network appliances, management interfaces, and end-of-life PHP systems now. For the rest of your PHP estate, patch on your critical schedule, and check that less publicized vulnerabilities that are easy to exploit in your environment are not waiting behind php2shell.

Title: Brotli2Shell: Frequently asked questions for Google Brotli decoder vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497)
Context: A list of Tenable plugins for this vulnerability can be found on the individual CVE page for CVE-2026-111497 as they're released
Full Text:
Researchers have demonstrated remote code execution through CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder library, and public proofs-of-concept (PoCs) are available. Software that uses the decoder includes Node.js, .NET, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Python HTTP clients and PHP for Windows.

Change log

Update October 28: Added a section on how reliable exploitation of CVE-2026-111497 has been so far, based on research from ELLIO and Imperva.

Click here to review the change log history

Update October 28: Added a section on how reliable exploitation of CVE-2026-111497 has been so far, based on research from ELLIO and Imperva.

Update October 27: CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its KEV catalog.

October 26: Original publication.

Key Takeaways

CVE-2026-111497, known as Brotli2Shell and by several other names, is an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder library that Google, the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), scored 9.2 under CVSSv4.0.

Any application that decompresses attacker-controlled data with a vulnerable Brotli decoder is potentially at risk, including Node.js, .NET, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Python HTTP clients, FFmpeg, Apache Arrow and ClickHouse.

Patches are available for Google Brotli and the major runtimes, though some projects had not shipped a fixed release as of October 26, and applications that bundle their own copy of Brotli each need their own fix.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding Brotli2Shell, a vulnerability in Google's Brotli C decoder library, which Node.js, .NET and other software embed.

FAQ

What is Brotli2Shell?

Brotli2Shell is one of several names for CVE-2026-111497, a memory corruption flaw in Google's open-source Brotli compression library. Some researchers call it Node2Shell, after Node.js, which disclosed the flaw in its October 21 security advisory. Others use HTTP2Shell, since the same bug reaches HTTP software outside Node.js. It has circulated as Broccoli2Shell as well. We use Brotli2Shell because the bug sits in the Brotli decoder itself, not in any one downstream product.

What is the vulnerability associated with Brotli2Shell?

CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Google Brotli C decoder library.

CVE

Description

CVSSv4.0

CVE-2026-111497

Google Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write vulnerability

9.2

An attacker can trigger the flaw by getting an application to decompress crafted Brotli data. Two common paths are a compressed HTTP response sent to a client that decompresses it automatically, and a compressed request body sent to a server that decompresses incoming content. The impact ranges from a process crash to potential remote code execution, and the bug can also leak process memory.

Note on severity scoring: Google, as the CNA, scored the flaw 9.2 (CVSSv4.0) with vector CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N. Microsoft rates it 8.1 (CVSSv3.1) for .NET.

When was CVE-2026-111497 first disclosed?

Google committed the upstream fix to the Brotli source repository on February 27. Node.js publicly disclosed the vulnerability on October 21 in its security advisory, the same day Google released fixed Brotli versions. Envoy Proxy and Istio had already shipped fixed releases earlier in October without naming the flaw. NVD published the CVE record on October 22. Brotli 1.2.1 and brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 both reached the Python Package Index (PyPI) on October 22. On October 25, Microsoft released .NET security updates.

What software is affected by CVE-2026-111497?

The risk applies wherever an application decompresses Brotli data an attacker can control, whether that data arrives over HTTP in either direction or inside a file.

Node.js release lines that have reached end of support, including 20, 23 and 25, do not receive a fixed release. Akamai said its telemetry "shows that 61% of networks are running affected Node.js versions."

JFrog Security Research showed that the flaw also reaches FFmpeg through the libjxl library, by way of Brotli-compressed metadata in JPEG XL files. JFrog obtained instruction-pointer control in FFmpeg with a crafted JPEG XL file but did not demonstrate code execution. The same research produced an infinite-loop denial of service in Apache Arrow, which uses Brotli for compressed Parquet data, with a crafted 534-byte input, and crashed a tested ClickHouse server with a single malformed Brotli-compressed HTTP request. Python HTTP clients such as urllib3, requests, httpx and aiohttp are also in scope when the Brotli or brotlicffi package is installed.

Does updating the system Brotli library fix the issue?

It depends on where the software gets its decoder. Programs that load the operating system's copy of Brotli pick up the fix once they restart. Node.js, Bun and other applications that ship with a built-in copy keep the flawed decoder until a fixed release of that application is installed.

Is every .NET, Envoy Proxy or Istio installation exposed?

No. These platforms are exposed only when Brotli decompression is in use.

.NET: Microsoft says an application "is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed," and ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are off by default. Applications are in scope when they use ASP.NET Core request decompression, HttpClient response decompression, or the Brotli APIs in System.IO.Compression such as BrotliStream and BrotliDecoder. NativeAOT and self-contained applications pick up the fix only when they are rebuilt and redeployed. Microsoft says .NET Framework is not affected.

Envoy Proxy and Istio: Envoy Proxy is exposed only when its Brotli decompressor is configured, and Istio users are potentially affected when they enable Brotli decompression, for example through an EnvoyFilter. Istio 1.29 reached end of support on October 15. Its 1.29.9 release includes the fix.

Is PHP affected by CVE-2026-111497?

PHP's official Windows builds are affected, because they include their own copy of Brotli. On October 26, PHP released updated Windows builds that bundle Brotli 1.2.1. PHP names its cURL extension as the route to the flaw in those builds, once automatic decompression of HTTP responses is enabled. cURL keeps that setting off unless an application or HTTP client library enables it. On other platforms, PHP can still reach a vulnerable decoder through the system Brotli library or through the PHP brotli extension, which bundles its own copy and fixed the flaw in version 0.21.1. The PHP source releases are unchanged, and this flaw is separate from the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities covered in our FAQ.

Is CVE-2026-111497 being exploited in the wild?

On October 26, threat intelligence firm ELLIO reported that its sensors recorded an exploitation attempt against CVE-2026-111497. ELLIO said the attempt targeted Node.js 24.22.0 on x86-64 and combined code copied from public PoCs with an original exploit chain. Tenable has not independently confirmed this activity. On October 27, CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, with a remediation due date of November 10 for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies.

Has Tenable Research classified this vulnerability as part of Vulnerability Watch?

Yes. CVE-2026-111497 has been classified as a “Vulnerability of Interest” as part of Vulnerability Watch.

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available for CVE-2026-111497?

Yes. Public PoCs for CVE-2026-111497 are available on GitHub. The Imperva Red Team demonstrated code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image after multiple attempts, and has not released that exploit. At least one public PoC on GitHub claims code execution against Node.js 24.22.0 under narrow lab conditions. ELLIO said it reproduced code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 build on x86-64.

How reliable is exploitation of CVE-2026-111497?

According to ELLIO, an exploit has to be tuned to the specific Node.js build it targets. ELLIO reported that an exploit tuned for the official Node.js 24.22.0 build on x86-64 produced nothing in 10,000 attempts against Node.js 22.23.3 and 26.12.0, which each need their own memory offsets. Even against the matching build, most of ELLIO's 400 lab attempts against an Express server crashed the worker process instead of returning a shell, but where workers restart automatically, an attacker gets repeated tries. The exploit request ELLIO captured in the wild did not produce a shell in 50 lab attempts against a vulnerable Node.js 24.22.0 target. Imperva also needed multiple attempts to achieve code execution against Node.js 24.22.0 on Linux arm64.

Are patches or mitigations available for CVE-2026-111497?

Fixed versions for Google Brotli, Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, .NET, the Python Brotli packages and PHP for Windows are listed in the table above. As of October 26, ClickHouse had merged a fix without shipping a release, and the Apache Arrow issue remained open.

Patching does not reach code that is already running. The fixed decoder takes effect in a process or scheduled job only after a restart, and in a container only after its image is rebuilt and redeployed.

Where patching is delayed, the Patch the Planet mitigation guide and the broccoli2shell.com tracker list temporary steps that reduce exposure:

Blocking requests marked Content-Encoding: br at the proxy or load balancer, so they stop before anything decompresses them. This step does nothing for applications that fetch Brotli responses from attacker-controlled servers, and turning off Brotli compression on an origin server or CDN has no effect on decompression.

Turning off Brotli decoding in HTTP clients. Taking br out of the Accept-Encoding header falls short by itself, since a hostile server can still reply with Brotli-encoded data.

Disabling the Brotli decompressor filter in Envoy Proxy and Istio in both directions. A disabled filter forwards compressed bytes as they arrive, which leaves any downstream service that decodes Brotli at risk.

Removing the Brotli or brotlicffi package from Python environments until a patched version is in place.

Are there any indicators of compromise for CVE-2026-111497?

ELLIO published the source IP address and a payload hash for the exploitation attempt it observed. They are available in ELLIO's blog post.

Has Tenable released product coverage for CVE-2026-111497?

A list of Tenable plugins for this vulnerability can be found on the individual CVE page for CVE-2026-111497 as they're released. This link will display all available plugins for this vulnerability, including upcoming plugins in our Plugins Pipeline.

Title: [R1] Tenable Network Monitor 6.6.0 Fixes Multiple Vulnerabilities
Context: [R1] Tenable Network Monitor 6.6.0 Fixes Multiple Vulnerabilities Arnie Cabral Mon, 10/26/2026 - 1
Full Text:
[R1] Tenable Network Monitor 6.6.0 Fixes Multiple Vulnerabilities Arnie Cabral Mon, 10/26/2026 - 11:07

Tenable Network Monitor leverages third-party software to help provide underlying functionality. Several of the third-party components (OpenSSL, curl, expat, libxml2) were found to contain vulnerabilities, and updated versions have been made available by the providers.

Out of caution and in line with best practice, Tenable has opted to upgrade these components to address the potential impact of the issues. Tenable Network Monitor 6.6.0 updates OpenSSL to version 3.5.9, curl to version 8.21.0, expat to version 2.9.0 and libxml2 to version 2.15.4 to address the identified vulnerabilities.

Advanced Support Plan Features

Phone Support

Chat Support

Tenable Community Support Portal

All named support contacts can open support cases within the Tenable Community. Initial Response Time

Title: php2shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619): Frequently asked questions about critical PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities
Context: Two critical PHP vulnerabilities could lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. Patches are available for supported PHP 8.x branches, and exploitation attempts began before public disclosure.
Full Text:
Two critical PHP vulnerabilities could lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. Patches are available for supported PHP 8.x branches, and exploitation attempts began before public disclosure.

Change log

Update October 28: Clarified Amazon Threat Intelligence's wording to say php2shell is seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild. Added Dream Research's report of a campaign that chained php2shell with the Fragnesia Linux kernel flaw (CVE-2026-46300) to gain root access on firewalls.

Click here to review the change log history

Update October 28: Clarified Amazon Threat Intelligence's wording to say php2shell is seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild. Added Dream Research's report of a campaign that chained php2shell with the Fragnesia Linux kernel flaw (CVE-2026-46300) to gain root access on firewalls.

Update October 26: CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its KEV catalog. Added details on a regression in PHP 8.4.27 and 8.5.12 and on PHP's October 23 session upload progress advisory. Added a note on restarting PHP services after updating. Added Adel Karimi's report of successful exploitation against honeypot servers and Trail of Bits' report of working exploits against pre-patch PHP releases. Linked our Brotli2Shell FAQ for a separate fix in PHP's Windows builds.

Update October 23: Updated the Tenable Security Center and Tenable Enclave Security patch to SC-202610.2 and added a Tenable knowledge base article.

Update October 23: Added guidance on authenticated scanning and a dedicated view in Tenable Cloud Security. Reorganized the Tenable product coverage section.

Update October 23: Updated the example Tenable Hexa AI prompt.

Update October 22: Added security patch SC-202610.1 for Tenable Security Center and Tenable Enclave Security, plus a CyberAgents Exchange skill for reporting php2shell exposure. Added the status of these vulnerabilities in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog along with CISA's October 21 alert.

Update October 21: Added Amazon Threat Intelligence's report of exploitation attempts beginning October 17, before public disclosure. Added Tenable Nessus plugins, including local checks for PHP packages from Linux distributions, along with guidance on using Tenable Hexa AI to find vulnerable PHP installations and create remediation tickets.

Update October 21: PHP released patches and published its advisories. This post now includes vulnerability details, fixed versions, source backports for end-of-life branches, interim mitigation guidance, updated exploitation details and Tenable product coverage and Vulnerability Watch classification.

October 21: Original publication based on limited public information ahead of PHP's official advisory.

Key takeaways

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are critical vulnerabilities in PHP. The PHP security team rates both CVSSv4.0 9.2 and says they can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

Amazon Threat Intelligence observed an exploitation attempt on October 17, four days before public disclosure. It says php2shell "is now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild." On October 26, CISA added both CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

On October 21, 2026, PHP released fixes in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. End-of-life branches will not receive official releases, but the PHP security team published minimal source backports for PHP 7.4 through 8.1.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding two critical vulnerabilities in PHP that were announced on October 20, 2026.

FAQ

When were these PHP vulnerabilities first disclosed?

On October 20, 2026, the CVE identifiers circulated on Hacker News and social media. Later that day, the PHP security team published an advance notice of a security release scheduled for October 21 at 14:00 UTC (10:00 AM ET) to address two critical vulnerabilities. The notice said the team could release earlier if details became public or if exploitation appeared in the wild. CERT-EU also published an advisory (2026-018) naming both CVEs. According to the PHP Foundation, the release was originally scheduled for October 22 and was moved up by a day after the CVE identifiers leaked. On October 21, the PHP security team published its security advisory and released patches.

A video shared by researcher Kirill Firsov demonstrates the exploit chain, dubbed php2shell. Firsov credited the video and exploit to researcher LCFR of Calif.io, which has since published a technical writeup. The PHP Foundation credited Calif, OpenAI and Wiz, among others, for their research and responsible disclosure. Calif and Wiz have both said they used AI models in their research.

The PHP security team is giving advance notice: Upcoming security release Wed, Oct 21st 2026, 14:00UTC, two critical vulnerabilities, both rated CVSSv4 9.2.PHP users are encouraged to prepare to update. Earlier release if details become public or active exploit evidence.

— The PHP Foundation (@ThePHPF) October 20, 2026

What are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619?

CVE

Description

CVSSv4.0

CVE-2026-109618

PHP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (OOM Corruption)

9.2

CVE-2026-109619

PHP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (Stale Global State)

9.2

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in PHP. CVE-2026-109618 stems from how PHP handles out-of-memory (OOM) errors. If memory runs out while PHP's internal request data is only partially initialized, the cleanup that follows can treat that data as valid. CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw. Leftover state from one request points to freed memory, and a later request handled by the same worker can then use it. According to PHP, both can be exploited by an unauthenticated remote attacker. PHP's advisory for CVE-2026-109619 also lists memory disclosure as a confirmed impact.

PHP says every installation that serves web requests is at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. PHP considers the risk highest for mod_php, where a demonstrated exploit can be triggered by an unauthenticated request before any application code runs.

CVSS scores differ across sources. The PHP security team rates both vulnerabilities as CVSSv4.0 9.2. According to the PHP Foundation, the CVE identifiers that circulated before the release came with an incorrect CVSS score of 10.0.

Which PHP versions are affected?

According to Calif's technical writeup, the earliest affected code path it found dates to PHP 5.4.0. The PHP security team released the following fixed versions:

Affected Versions

Fixed Version

8.5.12

8.4.27

8.3.36

8.2.35

PHP 7.4.x through 8.1.x

No official release; minimal source backports from the PHP security team

PHP 5.4.x through 7.3.x

End-of-life, no fix from the PHP project

According to PHP, Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches in advance. If you use distribution packages, check your vendor's advisories.

On October 26, PHP released updated Windows builds, 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1 and 8.2.35-1, that fix a separate vulnerability in their bundled Brotli library, CVE-2026-111497. The PHP source and runtime versions are unchanged. For details, see our Brotli2Shell FAQ.

How widespread is PHP, and how many hosts are potentially affected?

According to W3Techs, PHP is used by 69.3% of websites whose server-side language is known. Platforms such as WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Laravel and Magento all run on PHP. Calif says it confirmed pre-authentication remote code execution against specific versions of popular PHP applications, including WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento. Security researcher Silas Cutler's rough estimate is that over 1.3 million internet-exposed hosts are potentially vulnerable. A Shodan search by Henk Poley counts over 1.9 million internet-exposed hosts running PHP.

Has exploitation been observed in the wild?

On October 21, Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht said the company is "seeing early attacks emerging" and is updating its mitigations as new attack vectors appear. watchTowr says it has reproduced both vulnerabilities and is observing exploitation attempts against both.

Amazon Threat Intelligence said it observed a php2shell exploitation attempt against its MadPot honeypot network on October 17, four days before public disclosure. It said it is unclear how the attacker obtained exploit information. More attempts followed on October 21, with payloads and infrastructure that Amazon says suggest multiple actors. Amazon says it is unclear whether any of the October 21 attempts would have succeeded against real-world systems. It also says php2shell "is now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild." It recommends starting investigations from at least October 17, not from the disclosure date.

On October 24, security researcher Adel Karimi reported successful exploitation against three honeypot servers running PHP 8.4.26. The exploit requests started shells that ran attacker commands. The report says the activity is consistent with CVE-2026-109618, and that it does not show use of CVE-2026-109619. It also says the traffic closely matches a family of publicly available proof-of-concept exploits. The honeypots used a single-worker Apache mod_php setup that was intentionally favorable to the exploit, and the report says the results are not a measure of how reliably the exploit works on other setups.

On October 26, Dream Research reported finding artifacts of a campaign that chained a custom php2shell exploit with CVE-2026-46300, a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw known as Fragnesia that we covered in a separate FAQ. According to Dream, the attacker gained root access on 24 internet-facing firewalls from an unnamed vendor, then used the same chain on an internal firewall management server reached through one of them. Some of these systems "appeared to belong to a US government-affiliated environment." Dream said the php2shell exploit was not a public one and needed precise memory offsets for each version of the firewall software. Dream has not named the vendor or the affected versions, and Tenable has not independently confirmed this activity.

PHP sites behind Cloudflare already have an initial set of WAF rules deployed for the known exploit vectors in these vulnerabilities. The rules are available to all customers, including free.We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up.This is a STOPGAP only. Patch as soon as @ThePHPF releases the update at 14:00 UTC today.

— Dane Knecht 🦭 (@dok2001) October 21, 2026

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available?

Code claiming to exploit these vulnerabilities is circulating publicly, but we have not verified that any of it works against CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619. Unverified exploit code is sometimes laced with malware, so treat it with caution. The PHP Foundation said the PHP security team inspected PoCs that appeared after the leak but "did not identify any functional exploits at the time of release/public disclosure."

Since then, on October 26, Trail of Bits said it confirmed that php2shell exploits work against pre-patch releases of PHP 8.2 through 8.5, and its demo showed a shell on MediaWiki, Symfony, Laravel and phpBB.

Are patches or mitigations available?

Yes. The PHP security team released fixed versions on October 21 (see the table above). For end-of-life branches, it published minimal source backports for PHP 7.4 through 8.1, for those who build from source. If you run another end-of-life version, upgrade to a supported release or ask your distribution or LTS vendor.

The PHP security team says updating is the only complete fix. For organizations that cannot update immediately, PHP's advisory lists configuration changes that reduce exposure to specific attack paths but do not make an installation safe. For CVE-2026-109618, PHP lists setting memory_limit=-1 in a way applications cannot override. For CVE-2026-109619, it lists setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and, on PHP 8.5, fatal_error_backtraces=0. PHP says to restart every PHP worker after these changes. PHP also suggests a container or cgroup memory limit as an availability boundary, though it says this is not a complete mitigation either.

Installing updated PHP packages does not patch PHP processes that are already running. Google Cloud's guidance, which includes input from Mandiant, notes that PHP-FPM, Apache and other services that run PHP keep the vulnerable code in memory until they are restarted. The same guidance says to capture worker memory from servers that show signs of probing before restarting them, because a restart erases that evidence.

CERT-EU also recommends that organizations that cannot update right away consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix is applied and verified.

Cloudflare has deployed WAF rules for the known exploit vectors, available to all customers including the free tier. Cloudflare describes this as a stopgap only. The rules only cover traffic routed through Cloudflare.

Are there known issues with the new PHP releases?

PHP developers confirmed a regression in PHP 8.4.27 and 8.5.12 that can crash PHP processes in some applications that use the SimpleXML extension. It is tracked as php-src issue #24488. PHP developers traced it to a separate garbage collector fix included in those releases, not to the patches for CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619. A fix has been merged into the PHP source but, as of October 26, has not shipped in a release.

On October 23, PHP published an informational advisory about what it calls an unlikely remote code execution vector in session upload progress, tracked as CVE-2026-115560. PHP says it only occurs under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. Until its next regular bugfix release, PHP suggests setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0, the same setting its CVE-2026-109619 advisory listed as a mitigation.

Have PHP vulnerabilities been exploited before?

Yes. Before php2shell, the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog included three vulnerabilities in PHP itself. Two of them are known to have been used in ransomware campaigns:

The third, CVE-2012-1823, is a PHP-CGI flaw that CVE-2024-4577 later bypassed.

Have these vulnerabilities been added to the CISA KEV catalog?

Yes. On October 26, CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to the KEV catalog, with a remediation due date of October 29 for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies.

Has Tenable Research classified these vulnerabilities as part of Vulnerability Watch?

Yes. CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 have been classified as “Vulnerability of Concern” as part of Vulnerability Watch.

Is Tenable affected by these vulnerabilities?

Tenable Security Center and Tenable Enclave Security include PHP. Out of caution, Tenable released stand-alone security patch SC-202610.2 for both products on October 23. It updates PHP to 8.2.35. Details are available in TNS-2026-30 for Tenable Security Center and TNS-2026-31 for Tenable Enclave Security. Tenable customers can find patch release notes in this knowledge base article. Advisories for Tenable products are published at tenable.com/security.

Has Tenable released any product coverage for these vulnerabilities?

Yes. The following Tenable Nessus plugin is available for these vulnerabilities:

Do scans need to be authenticated?

For PHP installed on hosts, credentialed or agent scans give the most complete results. Tenable Nessus plugin 369483 uses both local and remote checks. An unauthenticated scan can detect a vulnerable version only if the host exposes its PHP version over the network, so results vary by host. For web applications, Tenable One Web App Scanning plugins 115719 to 115722 work without authentication and check the PHP version the application exposes.

How can Tenable customers find affected assets?

Tenable One Vulnerability Management customers can use the Software tab in Explore to find assets running PHP. Filter by Product is equal to PHP, then compare each asset's PHP version against the fixed versions above. The tab is populated from scan results, so run credentialed or agent scans regularly to keep it current.

Customers can also use Tenable One Attack Surface Management to find public-facing assets running PHP with this query: Programming Languages contains PHP.

Tenable Cloud Security now has a dedicated view for PHP2Shell. It lists every detected instance of these vulnerabilities, and customers can filter or group results to find affected virtual machines and images, including AMIs and container images. Customers can find it under Risk > Emerging Threats.

Tenable One customers can also use Tenable Hexa AI to find assets running vulnerable PHP versions in their organization and automatically create remediation tickets.

Customers using the Tenable Hexa AI MCP can use the PHP2Shell Tenable Skill and other open-source AI agents available on the CyberAgents Exchange. The skill is read-only and produces a php2shell exposure report in HTML and PDF, with a CSV export.
